edges.description: Conditional Atg7 knockout reproduces the brain abnormalities and the hypotonia and muscle weakness seen in patients.
edges.limitations: Systemic Atg7-null mice die within 24 hours of birth whereas the patients survive into adulthood, so the model does not reproduce the natural history or viability of the human disorder. The conditional design also bypasses the developmental context in which the human phenotype arises.

nodes.description: The clinical syndrome: mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, motor and language developmental delay, ataxia and tremor as common features across families, with axial hypotonia and spastic diplegia in some patients and psychiatric involvement in others.

evidence.snippet: The clinical course for all the surviving siblings has been similar, with mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, motor and language developmental delay, ataxia, and tremor being common features.

nodes.description: The neurodevelopmental consequence. Every patient with available MRI had cerebellar hypoplasia and corpus callosum abnormality, most characteristically a thin posterior corpus callosum; in some the effect on brain development was more diffuse, with diffuse brain volume loss. Additional structural findings included bilateral optochiasmatic atrophy.

nodes.description: Conditional Atg7 ablation in nerve and muscle produces ataxia and myopathy respectively, and the conditional knockouts reproduce several of the human clinical features. Systemic Atg7-null mice, by contrast, die within 24 hours of birth.
Endocrine involvement included late-onset or absent puberty and, in one patient, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with gynecomastia, suggesting a role for ATG7 in human endocrine development.

evidence.reference_title: Developmental Consequences of Defective ATG7-Mediated Autophagy in Humans.
evidence.snippet: ATG7 may play a role in human endocrine development: patients from Family 2 had late-onset or no puberty, and Patient 5 presented with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and gynecomastia.

nodes.description: ATG7 activates ATG12 before its conjugation to ATG5, which promotes expansion of the preautophagosomal phagophore, and it facilitates lipidation of LC3-I with phosphatidylethanolamine to generate LC3-II. LC3-II sits on the inner and outer autophagosomal membranes and recruits cytoplasmic cargo directly or through selective adaptor proteins. Without ATG7 both conjugation systems fail, so the phagophore cannot expand and cargo cannot be marked for capture.

nodes.description: Patient cells show impaired autophagic flux and markedly reduced autophagic sequestration. Importantly this is a severe reduction, not a complete abolition: evidence of basal autophagy was readily identified in patient fibroblasts and skeletal muscle despite loss of ATG7. This residual activity is the likely explanation for human survival and is curated as an open question rather than asserted as a mechanism.

nodes.description: Biallelic deleterious ATG7 variants diminish or abolish the ATG7 protein. ATG7 is the E1-like activating enzyme at the head of both ubiquitin-like conjugation systems that build the autophagosome, and it has no known functional paralogue, so its loss is not buffered.

nodes.description: Muscle biopsy showed mild myopathic changes, and patients had proximal muscle weakness and hypotonia. Notably the changes are mild: no vacuoles or internalized nuclei were present and electron microscopy showed normal muscle-fibre organization, so this is not a vacuolar myopathy.

nodes.description: p62 (SQSTM1) is the classical autophagy cargo receptor: it recruits cytoplasmic cargo to autophagosomes through interaction with LC3-II and is itself degraded after autolysosome formation. When LC3-II cannot be generated, p62 is neither consumed nor able to deliver cargo, and it accumulates. This is the cardinal cellular readout that failed lipidation has actually blocked cargo degradation, and it is the practical diagnostic biomarker alongside the LC3-II immunoblot.
